title: Springfield band, the drunken pianist, Don Albert and Kid Rena's trick
summary: Handy describes his Springfield band, a brilliant piano player who was always drunk, seeing Don Albert, and being tripped up by Kid Rena at the fairgrounds.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: What were the names of the other people?
You don't know? I can't remember. They were New Orleans people?

No. One of the boys was from Springfield. His name was Johnny. Johnny something. He was the drummer. I had a little fellow from Los Angeles, California playing piano. I can't think of his name right off. But he was a wonderful piano player. He got his hands with Sue Lily. He had to take this hard paper like that and wrap it around his sandwich with rubber to make it sound. Rubber to make it make tense on the piano. The only way he can make tense on the piano. The only way he can make tense on the piano. Put a piece of paper on his finger to make his finger long enough so he can make tense on the piano.

Well, he had a little bit of air on the piano. But play. Ooh, he could play some piano. And never was sober. Never was sober. He stayed right there in the same hotel with us. He wake up in the morning and get drunk. Get drunk when he eat. Twelve o'clock he get drunk. Go to work he's drunk. Come from work he's drunk. But play. Never was late on the job. And never went to sleep. Never went to sleep. But he'd be drunk. Played everything you put in front of him and what you don't put in front of him he played. He was a wonderful guy. I remember one night him and the taxi cab driver after they'd taken us home. By the way, that's where I met Don Albert in Springfield. You didn't know him down here. You didn't know him down here, huh? Yeah, I know him down here. But I hadn't seen him in about three, four years. He had Alvin Alcorn with him then. And a drummer from around there used to call him Fat. He died up in Texas a couple years ago. He was playing with me when he left with me when he left with Don Albert in Springfield. And Alvin Alcorn was playing with me on the Pelican. And they left him with Don. What was a Pelican? What was a Pelican? I was on Gravy and Ramport. Just a big dance hall. One of the bigger dance halls was around here at that time. I remember when I first come here to New Orleans. These guys used to have a habit of stuff with stuff When they want you tricky on the bandstand, they let you get up there and blow your tops. And then the trumpet player would slip his trumpet out at ease. And knock off a number. Now you find it. Renee did me that out at the fairground. I was out there. I played five or six numbers. People all gathering around and staring. Carrying on and clapping and raising. And Renee slipped that trumpet in the air on me. And knocked off high society. I couldn't find no, no, no kind of way. And I know I had been playing with the, Fate on the jam sessions, Fate Marvel. Fate Marvel start a number and one sharp and run it all the way to the seven. And he'd come back, right back and start a number one flat and run all the way to seven flats. And I was in the jam session. But he never did lose me. But Renee lost me in high society. I was in the high society. I couldn't get in there nowhere in the world. I never did forget that either. Did you play much with Renee? Oh yeah, I played a lot with Renee. As a matter of fact, he tried all kinds of ways to get me to join his band. I wouldn't leave Tom Alvin. He had a nice, he had a nice, uh, clarinet player with him. A fellow by the name of Zeb. Playing clarinet with him.
